title: Protecting your edges and hairline
question_forms: How do I protect my edges and hairline?
tradition_says: Edges are the fine hair at the temples and hairline. They are said to be fragile, to need edge control and a brush, and to be protected by keeping hair slicked down and moisturised.

layer1.plain_answer: Edges thin mainly from pulling: tight styles, glue on the hairline and frequent heat are linked to hairline loss. Caught early and with the pulling stopped, hair can regrow within months; long-standing loss can be permanent. Edge products have not been tested. If your edges are thinning, see a doctor early.

do.text: Keep styles loose at the hairline, or leave the edges out of braids.

source.name: British Association of Dermatologists, patient leaflet "Caring for Afro-textured hair" (July 2023)

do.text: Put adhesive just in front of the hairline, not on it.

source.name: British Association of Dermatologists, patient leaflet "Caring for Afro-textured hair" (July 2023)

do.text: If edges are thinning, stop the pulling style: regrowth may start about 3 months later.

source.name: British Association of Dermatologists, patient leaflet "Traction alopecia"

do.text: Protect thinning areas from the sun with sunscreen or a hat.

source.name: British Association of Dermatologists, patient leaflet "Traction alopecia"

do.text: Limit heat on hair at the hairline.

source.name: British Association of Dermatologists, patient leaflet "Caring for Afro-textured hair" (July 2023)

avoid.text: Heat-styling many times a month: more than two sessions a month carried higher odds of hairline recession.

source.name: American Academy of Dermatology, "Black hair: tips for everyday care"

see_someone_when: Edges or temples thinning or receding (doctor, then dermatologist).
A smooth, shiny hairline with no visible hair openings (dermatologist soon: scarring).
Pain, bumps or itch at the hairline that does not settle (doctor).

tested.population: 574 African schoolgirls (6-21 years) and 604 women (18-86 years), South Africa
tested.design: Two population studies analysed together; logistic regression
tested.finding: Traction alopecia was present in 17.1% of schoolgirls and 31.7% of women. Risk was highest when traction was added to relaxed hair (odds ratio 3.47 against natural hair, 95% CI 1.94-6.20).

source.authors: Khumalo NP, Jessop S, Gumedze F, Ehrlich R
source.journal: Journal of the American Academy of Dermatology

tested.population: 197 Ghanaian women, mean age 23, hairline status scored on the Marginal Traction Alopecia Score
tested.finding: 40.6% had hairline recession consistent with traction alopecia. More than two high-frequency heat-styling sessions a month was associated with higher odds (adjusted odds ratio 5.65, 95% CI 1.35-23.62). Keeping one hairstyle for over 6 weeks showed higher estimated odds that were not significant (1.81, 95% CI 0.59-5.60).

tested.design: Development and reliability test of a severity score
tested.finding: The Marginal Traction Alopecia Severity score divides the scalp margins into regions so that hairline loss can be measured. The authors state that traction alopecia is common in African females.
tested.note: A measurement tool, not an outcome study.

tier_driver: That hairline loss tracks with traction and frequent heat: cross-sectional studies in African girls and women.
tier_note: Observational and cross-sectional, none randomised; the 2026 Ghanaian survey is small. Edge-control products and brushes have no study.
harm_note: Hairline recession in 41% of 197 Ghanaian women (Ayugane 2026) and traction alopecia that can become permanent (BAD leaflet).
evidence_summary: In 1,178 African girls and women, traction alopecia was found in 17% of girls and 32% of women, highest when tension was added to relaxed hair (Khumalo 2008). A hairline score (M-TAS) exists to measure marginal loss (Khumalo 2007). In 197 Ghanaian women, more than two high-frequency heat sessions a month carried higher odds of hairline recession (adjusted odds ratio 5.65, 1.35 to 23.62). The British leaflet says regrowth may start about 3 months after the pulling stops but long-standing cases can be permanent, and lists topical minoxidil as a treatment that may help.
gaps: Untested: edge brushes, gels and growth products; the safest hairline treatment of braids; whether minoxidil works on traction hairline loss in a trial (the BAD leaflet says it may help; no trial opened).
